blogs.title: The 'Central Reason' Trap: How Mixed Motives Doomed the Jimenez Family's Political Asylum Claim
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Tenth Circuit's rigorous application of the 'one central reason' standard in mixed-motive asylum cases. It dissects how the court distinguished between the petitioners' political activism (which generated initial threats) and their subsequent conflict with a narco-trafficker over a property dispute. The analysis focuses on why the court deemed political opinion merely 'tangential' compared to the financial and security interests of the persecutor, offering practical guidance for practitioners on how to plead nexus in complex scenarios where criminal enterprises intersect with political dissent.

blogs.title: Threats Without Harm: Reaffirming the High Bar for 'Past Persecution' in Private Violence Cases
blogs.description: Focusing on the threshold element of asylum eligibility, this article examines the court's rejection of the petitioners' claim that threats, psychological trauma, and a brief abduction attempt constituted 'past persecution.' The post explores the Tenth Circuit's consistent doctrine that emotional distress and verbal threats—even when severe—are insufficient absent physical harm or significant restrictions on liberty. It discusses the tension between evolving understandings of psychological injury and established circuit precedent, citing *Karki* and *Chhetri* to illustrate why this specific fact pattern falls short of statutory requirements.

blogs.title: The Reporting Imperative: Why Failure to Seek Police Protection Fatalized Claims Against Narco-State Actors
blogs.description: This piece delves into the procedural hurdle of establishing that a government is 'unable or unwilling' to protect its citizens. It critiques the petitioners' strategy of avoiding police contact based on a generalized belief that corrupt officials were complicit with their persecutors. The analysis highlights how the court utilized the lack of specific reporting attempts—and contradictory evidence that authorities had successfully raided the persecutor's compound—to dismantle claims of state acquiescence. This serves as a critical reminder for litigants about the necessity of documenting futility rather than assuming it.
